coherence.reasons: Both run a clean diagnosis → levers → plan → sequencing → risks hierarchy, and their titles are supported by the evidence beneath them. X is tightly pyramided, but its governing thought says "not wages" while targeted labor is its largest single lever ($7.3M) and sits in the first wave, ahead of the shrink program its own diagnosis ranks higher. Its headline 3.2% is also stated before a known 2027 wage rise that its own backup shows drops the plan to 2.7%. Y's sequencing follows its diagnosis: promotions, delivery and shrink first, labor second, exits third. Its one tension is a title promising "~3%" when identified levers reach 2.8%, but the executive summary and the decision page state this openly.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend a defensible R1/R2-type plan: prune promotions, reprice delivery, fix shrink, grow private label, exit weak stores and cut labor only where shrink is low. Y weighs the trade-offs more soberly. It puts the 2027 wage rise in the base case and tells the board that identified levers reach 2.8%, with $3.4M of named stretch needed to hit 3.0%. It quantifies the draft plan's outcome (~1.5%, range 1.0–2.0%) as a real alternative. It notes that store-exit run-rate may land only in FY2029, proposes rent renegotiation before closure, flags uncosted one-time items against the $25M cap, and seeks in-principle approval for the three long-lease exits with store-level cases to follow. It also holds delivered volume flat until orders cover cost. X weighs the 8% versus 4% labor options and the six versus nine store exits well, and it protects promotions near ValuMart. But its base case leaves out the known wage rise, assumes all exits are in run-rate by FY2028, and rests the target on stretch levers only in a risk table.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: e-commerce at −$10.4M, −$12.34 per delivered order and −$1.64 per pickup; store exits at $6.6M with a 3.4-year payback; and the wage-versus-hours decomposition. Y gives the bridge in both points and dollars (−$12.6M, −$10.5M, −$7.5M, −$4.5M, −$3.0M, +$2.7M, +$2.8M), which matches the key. It adds a break-even test showing e-commerce loses money unless more than 70% of its sales are new, and a break-even test for promotions. It reconciles the 6.1% claim to the $8.3M of net delivery cost, and its FY2026 covenant phasing is built up from stated assumptions that check out. X's arithmetic is also sound, and it does two things Y does not: it rebuilds the fulfillment line from order data and names the store-mix confound in the category team's claim. But X makes a weaker inference, that promotions "have not held off ValuMart", without a counterfactual. Its wage-rise scenario figures are slightly inconsistent ($7.3M, $37.9M, $45.8M). Its covenant test is a simple ratio with no phasing.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise the CFO/COO hypothesis. Each shows labor is about an eighth of the decline, that the fall in hours offset roughly 70% of the wage effect, and that an 8% cut could give back about half its saving through shrink. Each replaces it with a targeted cut of about 4% in Q3–Q4 stores, keeping the part of the hypothesis that survives. Y goes one step further by projecting the whole draft plan to FY2028 (~1.5%, or 1.0% if shrink rises) and stating that the e-commerce freeze leaves the ~$10M loss in place. X's side-by-side table of the 8% and 4% options is strong, but it addresses the freeze only implicitly.

overall.reasons: Both documents would serve the CEO well and share the same diagnosis and lever set. Y is the more reliable board document. Its bridge is in dollars and ranks the drivers correctly, and its base case absorbs the known wage rise and says plainly that the target needs stretch levers. It benchmarks the draft plan, builds the covenant outlook from phasing assumptions, tracks one-time costs against the $25M cap, and ends with four specific decisions. X is thorough and accurate on most numbers, and it handles the category team's claim well. But its headline 3.2% depends on leaving out a known cost and on all nine exits being in full run-rate by FY2028, and it takes about twice the length to reach the same decision.
